canonical_statement: The study proposes MoNe, a lightweight modular neural-memory plugin intended to extend frozen pretrained Transformers to long contexts without retraining the backbone.

MoNe separates context processing from query inference: it processes context segments with test-time learning, then answers queries by reading the resulting memory without rereading the original context.
The context is divided into non-overlapping segments of fixed length T=512 tokens and consumed sequentially.
Each selected Transformer decoder layer receives a fast-weight neural memory implemented as a SwiGLU multilayer perceptron with input, gating, and output weights updated during context processing.

At query time the memory maps query representations to a fixed set of memory-derived key-value tokens that are concatenated with the query attention inputs, so the number of memory key-value entries does not grow with stored context length.
MoNe trains small LoRA adapters and memory meta-parameters offline while keeping the pretrained Transformer backbone frozen; the learned meta-parameters are fixed during test-time memory updates.
The fast-weight memory uses an associative objective based on the negative inner product between the memory output for a key and its target value.
Test-time gradients are localized within each memory-augmented layer and do not propagate through other Transformer layers.
MoNe applies rotary positional embeddings within each context segment and reuses positions 0 through T-1 for every segment, while query positions also begin at zero.
After context processing, the final fast-weight memory state can be reused for multiple queries and extended by processing additional context segments.
Evaluation uses three RULER retrieval-oriented tasks: single needle-in-a-haystack, multi-key needle-in-a-haystack, and frequent-word extraction.
Single-needle and multi-key retrieval are scored with substring exact match, while frequent-word extraction is scored with variable recall.

canonical_statement: Offline training data are generated only at context lengths from 1K through 4K tokens, with 30,000 samples generated for each N in {2,...,8}.
All experiments use a frozen Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct backbone; the memory uses four heads with hidden size 224 and LoRA rank 128 with alpha 128.
Adding MoNe to the Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct backbone increases the parameter count by 6.4%.

canonical_statement: At 128K on MK-NIAH, using MoNe on all 24 layers scores 0.94, compared with 0.70 for the last 16 layers and 0.02 for the last 8 layers.
At 128K, MoNe uses 149.1 trillion FLOPs with all 24 memory layers, 132.6 trillion with the last 16 layers, and 116.1 trillion with the last 8 layers.
At 128K on MK-NIAH, segment size 512 scores 0.94, segment size 256 scores 0.75, and segment size 128 scores 0.53.

The ablation results show that reducing the number of memory-augmented layers or shortening segments can reduce computation, but the tested reductions substantially degrade long-context retrieval accuracy, especially beyond 32K.
The experiments use only Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct and controlled RULER retrieval tasks; larger model scales, natural long-document question answering, and conversational histories are not evaluated.
The paper reports FLOPs and peak GPU memory but does not provide wall-clock latency measurements for context compilation or query serving.

The authors conclude that modular neural memory can shift long-context cost into a reusable context-processing step while keeping query cost independent of stored context length in their architecture.
